oil.summary: Crude pulled back sharply Monday despite a month that has seen WTI gain more than 10% and Brent over 6%. Brent fell nearly 5% to $111/bbl and heating oil shed almost 5% as well, with RBOB off 2.2%, suggesting some profit-taking after October's geopolitical risk premium was partially priced in. The supply picture remains deeply fractured: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline threaten a key export artery, while U.S. forces report escorting 1.5 billion barrels through the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began. Saudi output jumped 12.2% in September to 8 million bpd, signalling Riyadh has abandoned its traditional production discipline. Meanwhile, the Trump administration's Russia diesel deal — ramping Russian refinery output under U.S.-approved export quotas — is adding supply on the distillates side, but drawing sharp political criticism. BPCL's planned cut to Russian crude imports adds another demand-side wrinkle heading into November.
drivers: Houthi attacks on Saudi East-West pipeline threaten Gulf export infrastructure, keeping a geopolitical risk floor under crude
Saudi Arabia surged output to 8 million bpd in September, signalling a departure from prior supply discipline and adding bearish medium-term pressure
Trump-Russia diesel deal boosts distillate supply via Russian refiners, weighing on heating oil; BPCL cutting Russian crude purchases reshapes Asian flow dynamics

gas.summary: Natural gas markets delivered a dramatic session. Henry Hub surged 14.73% in a single day to $3.028/MMBtu — an outsized move for a front-month contract — even as the one-month trend remains down 5.2%, pointing to a sudden near-term catalyst rather than a structural reversal. European TTF climbed a further 2.4% to €96.085/MWh, extending a brutal 33% one-month rally. The IEA's Fatih Birol warned that energy prices are unlikely to return to pre-war levels through 2027, framing the current dislocation as structural. The Iran war's impact on LNG is quantified in one headline at an added $39 billion to the global LNG bill. On the corporate side, EQT's $50 billion all-stock acquisition of Range Resources signals producers are betting on sustained record U.S. gas demand, consolidating Appalachian production at scale.
drivers: Henry Hub spiked nearly 15% intraday, likely driven by Iran conflict spillover tightening near-term U.S. supply expectations and LNG diversion pressures
TTF extended its month-long 33% rally as the Middle East conflict continues to disrupt global LNG flows, with the Iran war estimated to have added $39 billion to the world's LNG bill
EQT's $50 billion acquisition of Range Resources signals industry conviction in structurally elevated U.S. gas demand, accelerating Appalachian consolidation

power.summary: EU carbon allowances edged up 2.3% to $84.14/EUA, continuing a modest but steady climb — up 3.1% on the week and 1.8% on the month — broadly consistent with elevated European gas prices feeding through to higher carbon costs for gas-fired generation. TTF at €96.085/MWh, up 33% over the past month, is the dominant cost driver for European power producers and is sustaining carbon demand from utilities that cannot yet switch fuels. The IEA's Birol cautioned that elevated energy prices will persist well into 2027, removing any near-term relief narrative for power-sector consumers. Headline flow for this sector is relatively thin today beyond the macro energy-price backdrop; the EQT-Range deal and the ongoing Middle East conflict are the primary indirect influences on European power and carbon pricing.
drivers: TTF's 33% monthly surge continues to push up marginal generation costs for European gas-fired power, sustaining EUA demand
IEA's Birol explicitly ruled out a return to pre-war energy price levels in 2027, anchoring a structurally elevated carbon price outlook
Dedicated power and carbon-specific news flow is thin today; price action largely reflects pass-through from persistently high European gas markets
